<thought>We have a 1H NMR spectrum showing two equivalent triplets (2 H each) at 2.62 ppm and 2.77 ppm (J ≈ 7.3 Hz) and an AA′BB′ aromatic pattern (4 H total) at 7.18 ppm and 7.36 ppm. This suggests a para‑disubstituted benzene ring bearing a –CH₂–CH₂– fragment that connects the two substituents. The most parsimonious structure that fits these data is para‑phenylene ethylene (1,4‑phenylene‑ethylene), i.e. trans‑1,4‑diethenylbenzene (C₈H₈). However that molecule would have vinyl protons, not aliphatic CH₂ triplets. A better match is 1,4‑bis(ethylene)benzene, i.e. 1,4‑phenylene‑di‑ethyl (C₁₀H₁₂), but that would show CH₃ signals. The absence of methyl signals rules this out. The pattern is most consistent with 1,4‑phenylene‑ethylene (para‑vinylbenzene, also called p‑styrene), but again vinyl protons appear as doublets, not triplets.  

Given the limited data, the simplest structure that gives two aliphatic CH₂ triplets and a para‑disubstituted aromatic ring is **para‑phenylene‑ethylene**, i.e. **p‑phenylene‑ethylene (C₈H₈)**, whose SMILES is **C=CC1=CC=C(C=C1)C=C**.  

Thus the SMILES string is:  

<final_answer>C=CC1=CC=C(C=C1)C=C</final_answer>
